drills.q: Name the four distinct ML test layers and, in one phrase, what each validates that the others don't.
drills.a: Data tests: is the training/serving input itself trustworthy (schema, nulls, label balance) before any model is trained. Model tests: does the model meet a performance bar per SLICE, not just in aggregate. Behavioral tests (CheckList-style): does the model have a specific capability, independent of whether aggregate accuracy happened to cover it. Metamorphic tests: does a defined input-output relation hold, without needing ground-truth labels for the perturbed case -- plus ongoing production drift monitoring as a fifth, continuous layer.

drills.q: Explain CheckList's three test types (MFT, INV, DIR) with an example of a bug each is specifically designed to catch.
drills.a: MFT (Minimum Functionality Test): a simple, targeted example checking a basic capability exists, e.g. 'I don't like this' correctly predicted negative -- catches outright capability gaps. INV (Invariance): a label-preserving perturbation like swapping a name shouldn't change the prediction -- catches spurious correlations/shortcut learning (e.g. the model secretly keys off names correlated with sentiment in training data). DIR (Directional Expectation): adding a clear negative clause to a positive review should lower the positive score -- catches a model that's sensitive to input but not sensitive in the correct direction, a subtler failure than the other two.

drills.q: A model posts 0.90 aggregate AUC and ships, then is found post-launch to discriminate badly against an 8%-of-traffic minority slice sitting at 0.65 AUC. Diagnose the testing gap and the fix.
drills.a: The evaluation only checked aggregate AUC and never sliced results by the relevant demographic/segment dimension -- the aggregate metric mathematically dilutes a minority slice's poor performance into near-invisibility when that slice is a small fraction of the overall test set. Fix: add per-slice model tests as a required promotion gate, with slices chosen deliberately (known sensitive attributes, known underrepresented segments) rather than whatever the evaluation script happens to compute by default.

drills.q: Why is metamorphic testing particularly valuable for fairness testing specifically, compared to a standard labeled model test?
drills.a: Metamorphic testing asserts a RELATION between an input perturbation and the expected output change (e.g., swapping the gender field on a credit application shouldn't increase predicted default risk) without requiring a ground-truth label for the perturbed, counterfactual input. Standard labeled model tests can't be constructed for these cases because a real, labeled 'correct' outcome for a hypothetical counterfactual applicant usually doesn't exist -- metamorphic relations sidestep that requirement entirely.

drills.q: Distinguish data drift from concept drift, and explain why concept drift is the more dangerous of the two to monitor for.
drills.a: Data drift is a shift in the input feature distribution (e.g. average customer age rising over time); concept drift is a shift in the actual relationship between inputs and the correct output (the same input now genuinely warrants a different prediction due to a real-world change). Concept drift is more dangerous because it can occur with NO detectable shift in the input distribution -- distributional monitoring (PSI, KS test) alone would completely miss it, which is why downstream performance/business-metric monitoring must be paired with distributional monitoring rather than substituted for it.

drills.q: What do PSI thresholds conventionally mean, where does the convention come from, and why is PSI generally preferred over a raw KS-test p-value for production monitoring?
drills.a: PSI < 0.1 conventionally means no significant drift, 0.1-0.25 means moderate drift warranting investigation, and > 0.25 means significant drift warranting action -- a convention originating in credit-risk scorecard monitoring in financial services, now applied broadly. PSI is generally preferred over a raw KS-test p-value in production because KS-test significance becomes oversensitive at the large sample sizes typical of production traffic, flagging even trivially small, practically irrelevant distribution shifts as 'statistically significant,' whereas PSI's binned, magnitude-based score gives a more actionable, practically interpretable signal.

drills.q: A PSI-based drift alert fires on a feature that turns out to be a benign seasonal pattern (e.g. holiday shopping). What monitoring design flaw caused this, and how do you fix it without losing the ability to catch real drift?
drills.a: The reference distribution was likely a single static training-time snapshot that didn't account for known cyclical/seasonal variation, so a normal seasonal shift got flagged identically to genuine concerning drift. Fix by comparing against a reference window that accounts for known seasonality (e.g. this December vs. last December) or tracking PSI trend across comparable periods, rather than one static forever-baseline -- while still tracking a shorter-window trend in parallel so a large deviation from both signals is treated as the stronger, more trustworthy alert.

drills.q: Why can't a CheckList-style behavioral test suite be produced by mechanically running a generic template, and what specifically made CheckList's own published results (2x tests, 3x bugs found) strong?
drills.a: The value came from practitioners applying real, task-specific domain judgment to decide which linguistic/behavioral capabilities and perturbations actually matter for their particular model's use case -- a generic template run without that judgment produces shallow coverage, because deciding 'what capability matters here' and 'what perturbation would a real edge case or adversary produce' are domain questions no generic tool can answer on its own. CheckList provides the matrix/vocabulary and tooling, but the demonstrated bug-finding yield required practitioners to fill it in with real task understanding.

drills.q: A stakeholder says 'you told me the model passed testing' after a specific behavioral capability (e.g., sarcasm handling) that the business cares about is found to fail badly, despite passing data and per-slice model tests. How do you explain this without implying testing is unreliable in general?
drills.a: Explain that 'passed testing' was never one binary claim -- data and model tests validate that training data was clean and the model meets a statistical performance bar on held-out data, which is necessary but says nothing about specific behavioral capabilities that may be underrepresented in that held-out data's distribution. Behavioral testing is a distinct, additional, cumulative layer specifically because a model can be statistically strong in aggregate while having a systematic capability gap the other layers structurally can't see. If behavioral tests genuinely weren't run before this point, own that as a real process/coverage gap directly, rather than implying it was an unavoidable limitation of ML testing as a discipline.

drills.q: Leadership wants to reduce ML testing investment because aggregate metrics have been stable for two years. What's the strongest response, grounded in the specific blind spots stable aggregate metrics have?
drills.a: Two years of stable aggregate metrics is weak evidence of true system health for two specific, named reasons: aggregate metrics structurally can't reveal slice-level degradation (a slice could silently worsen while other slices compensate to keep the aggregate flat), and stable input distributions don't rule out concept drift (the input-output relationship can shift with no detectable change in input distribution). The response should name the cost asymmetry rather than argue 'test more' on principle: continuous per-slice and drift monitoring are comparatively cheap and ongoing, while an undetected fairness incident or a silent concept-drift-driven business decline is expensive and typically discovered late -- propose keeping the cheap continuous monitoring layers while being open to scaling back the more expensive behavioral-suite-authoring effort only if the task's capability surface has genuinely stopped changing.
